title: Advance care planning and DNACPR
blurb: Make sure DNACPR and advance care decisions for people with a learning disability are individual, lawful and made with the person or those who know them, never because of the disability.
question: Martin, 46, has a severe learning disability and is admitted with a chest infection. A junior doctor writes on a DNACPR form: 'Reason: learning disability, poor quality of life.' Martin's sister, his main carer, has not been contacted. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: NHS England (letter C1146, 4 March 2021) is clear: people should not have a DNACPR on their record just because they have a learning disability, autism or both. The terms 'learning disability' and 'Down's syndrome' should never be a reason for a DNACPR order or be used to describe the underlying or only cause of death. Blanket policies, by condition, disability or age, are inappropriate. In plain English: every decision is about this person, their health and their wishes.

If the person has capacity, there is a presumption they will be consulted before a DNACPR decision unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as causing them harm (Tracey, 2014, Article 8). If the person lacks capacity, the MCA s4(7) requires the decision-maker to consult, where practicable and appropriate, anyone caring for the person or interested in their welfare. In Winspear (2015) placing a DNACPR on a man with cerebral palsy without consulting his mother, when it was practicable, breached Article 8.
teach.cite: Tracey [2014] EWCA Civ 822; Winspear [2015] EWHC 3250 (QB); MCA 2005 s4(7)

teach.caption: Paid support workers do not count as 'appropriate to consult' when deciding whether an IMCA is needed.

teach.body: Advance care planning is a voluntary process of conversations over time about what matters to the person and what they would want if they became seriously ill. NHS England notes some people need reasonable adjustments to take part: easy read and pictures, several shorter conversations, people who know their communication, and records the person can understand. A person who has capacity can make their own choices, including an advance decision to refuse treatment.

The stated reason is Martin's learning disability, which NHS England says is never a valid reason, and his sister, his main carer, has not been consulted. The nurse raises it with the consultant the same day, documents her concern and involves the learning disability liaison team. The consultant assesses Martin's capacity, makes an individual clinical judgement about whether CPR could succeed and, as Martin lacks capacity for this decision, consults his sister before any decision is recorded. The form is cancelled.

teach.text: Two traps. First, a clinician is not obliged to offer CPR that would not work, but the person (or, if they lack capacity, those close to them) should still be told and consulted, not just informed after the fact. Second, a DNACPR decision is about CPR only: it does not mean 'not for treatment', antibiotics, fluids, escalation or good nursing care.

rows.label: Involvement

items: Learning disability, autism or Down's syndrome are never reasons for DNACPR or the cause of death.
Blanket DNACPR decisions are inappropriate; each is individual.
Consult the person with capacity (Tracey); consult family and carers if they lack capacity (MCA s4(7), Winspear).
IMCA for serious medical treatment when there is no one but paid carers to consult.
A welfare LPA covers life-sustaining treatment only if it says so expressly.

summary: You can now recognise unlawful or discriminatory DNACPR decisions and escalate them. You can explain who must be involved in DNACPR and advance care decisions for people with and without capacity, and when an IMCA, LPA or ADRT applies.

A.q: Martin, 46, has a severe learning disability. A junior doctor writes on his DNACPR form: 'Reason: learning disability.' What should the nurse do?
options: Accept it, as the doctor has made a clinical decision
Ask Martin's sister to countersign the DNACPR form
File it in the notes and review it at discharge
Raise it with the consultant as an invalid reason
A.why: NHS England C1146: a learning disability should never be a reason for a DNACPR decision. The nurse escalates so an individual, lawful decision is made.

whyNot.0: A decision based on disability is discriminatory and against national guidance.
whyNot.1: A relative's signature does not make an invalid reason valid.
whyNot.2: Delaying review leaves an invalid decision in place.

A.q: A care home holds a list of residents with a learning disability marked 'not for CPR', made during a winter outbreak. What is the correct response?
options: Keep the list, as it was made by a doctor
Escalate it as an inappropriate blanket decision
Ask each family to agree to the list in writing first
Review the list at the end of the outbreak
A.why: Blanket DNACPR decisions applied to groups are inappropriate; each decision must be individual and made with the person or their family (NHS England C1146).

whyNot.0: Who wrote it does not make a blanket decision acceptable.
whyNot.2: Family agreement does not turn a group decision into an individual one.
whyNot.3: Leaving it in place until later risks harm now.

A.q: Kevin, 52, had a learning disability and has died of pneumonia. The doctor is completing the medical certificate of cause of death. What should be recorded?
options: Pneumonia and any conditions that led to it
Learning disability as the underlying cause
Learning disability and pneumonia equally
Natural causes linked to his disability
A.why: NHS England: 'learning disability' should never be used to describe the underlying or only cause of death. The illness that caused death is recorded so deaths can be understood and learned from.

whyNot.1: Learning disabilities are not fatal conditions.
whyNot.2: Listing the disability as a cause hides the learning from the death.
whyNot.3: Vague wording linked to disability obscures the real cause.

B.q: Ruth, 70, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to make decisions about CPR. The consultant decides CPR would not succeed. Her niece visits most days. What should happen before the decision is recorded?
options: Consult her niece where practicable and appropriate
Record the decision and tell her niece at her next visit
Ask Ruth's paid carers to agree the decision
Instruct an IMCA because Ruth lacks capacity
B.why: MCA s4(7) requires consultation with those caring for or interested in the person's welfare where practicable and appropriate; Winspear (2015) found failing to consult family before a DNACPR breached Article 8.

whyNot.1: Telling the family after the decision is not consultation.
whyNot.2: Paid carers can contribute but do not replace consulting family.
whyNot.3: An IMCA is needed only where there is no one appropriate to consult; her niece is available.

B.q: George, 55, has a learning disability and lacks capacity to decide about chemotherapy for bowel cancer. He has no family or friends; only paid support workers are involved. What must happen?
options: His support workers decide in his best interests
The consultant decides without consulting anyone
An IMCA must be instructed before the decision
The case must go to the Court of Protection
B.why: MCA s37: an NHS body must instruct an IMCA before serious medical treatment where the person lacks capacity and there is no one, other than paid carers, appropriate to consult.

whyNot.0: Paid carers do not count as appropriate to consult for this purpose.
whyNot.1: The decision-maker must consult; here that means an IMCA.
whyNot.3: Court is for disputes or certain serious cases, not the routine route here.

B.q: Tony, 60, has a learning disability and lacks capacity. His sister holds a registered health and welfare lasting power of attorney that expressly covers life-sustaining treatment. Who makes the CPR decision with the clinical team?
options: The consultant, acting alone
An IMCA appointed by the hospital
His GP, who knows him best
His sister, as his attorney
B.why: Under MCA ss9-11, a health and welfare attorney can make decisions about life-sustaining treatment if the LPA expressly authorises it, acting in Tony's best interests.

whyNot.0: A valid attorney with express authority is the decision-maker for this matter.
whyNot.1: An IMCA is not needed when an attorney is in place.
whyNot.2: The GP gives clinical input but is not the decision-maker.

C.q: Nina, 44, has a moderate learning disability and has capacity to discuss CPR. Her consultant believes CPR would not work and wants to avoid upsetting her by not mentioning it. What should happen?
options: Explain sensitively why CPR may not work and involve Nina
Record the DNACPR and explain it privately to her family instead
Ask Nina to sign a form without discussing the reasons
Delay any decision until she loses capacity
C.why: Tracey (2014): there is a presumption of consulting a patient with capacity about DNACPR unless there is a convincing reason not to. Avoiding upset is not enough; information is given accessibly.

whyNot.1: Telling family but not Nina breaches her right to be involved.
whyNot.2: A signature without understanding is not meaningful involvement.
whyNot.3: Waiting until she lacks capacity removes her voice.

C.q: Claire, 39, has a mild learning disability and a progressive illness. She has capacity and wants to plan her future care. What is the best approach?
options: Complete a ReSPECT form in a single meeting led by her parents and GP
Have accessible conversations over time and record her wishes
Ask her GP to decide what she would want later on
Wait until she is more unwell before starting
C.why: Advance care planning is a voluntary process over time. For people with a learning disability it uses accessible information and reasonable adjustments, recording the person's own wishes.

whyNot.0: A single meeting led by others does not centre Claire's wishes.
whyNot.2: The GP cannot decide for a person who has capacity.
whyNot.3: Delay risks losing the chance to plan while she can take part.

C.q: A nurse sees that Paul, 50, who has a learning disability, has a valid DNACPR decision. He now has sepsis, and a colleague says, 'He's DNACPR, so we won't escalate.' What should the nurse do?
options: Agree, as DNACPR means comfort care only
Ask his family whether they want the sepsis treated
Escalate his care, as DNACPR relates to CPR only
Wait for the consultant's ward round tomorrow
C.why: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR. All other appropriate treatment, including sepsis care and escalation, continues unless separately decided.

whyNot.0: DNACPR is not a 'not for treatment' or comfort-care-only order.
whyNot.1: Treatment of sepsis is a clinical decision; DNACPR does not transfer it to family.
whyNot.3: Sepsis needs urgent treatment; waiting is unsafe.

reteach.title: One person, one decision
reteach.question: What three questions should every DNACPR decision for a person with a learning disability answer?

blocks.body: Why: is the reason an individual clinical judgement about this person, never the disability itself? Who: was the person involved if they have capacity, or family and carers consulted if not (an IMCA if no one but paid carers)? What: is it clear the decision covers CPR only, with all other care continuing?

blocks.caption: A memory aid for this app.

blocks.text: A learning disability is not a terminal illness and not a cause of death. If you read it on a DNACPR form or death certificate, challenge it.

explain.body: NHS England C1146 (4 March 2021): no DNACPR just because of a learning disability, autism or both; 'learning disability' and 'Down's syndrome' never a reason or the cause of death; blanket policies inappropriate.

test.q: According to NHS England, which of these can be a reason for a DNACPR decision for a person with Down syndrome?
options: Their diagnosis of Down syndrome
Their age being over 50
An individual clinical judgement
A care home policy for residents
test.why: DNACPR decisions must be made on an individual basis; Down's syndrome is never a reason and blanket policies are inappropriate.

whyNot.0: NHS England says Down's syndrome should never be a reason.
whyNot.1: Blanket decisions by age are inappropriate.

explain.body: With capacity: consult the person unless there is a convincing reason not to (Tracey). Without capacity: consult those caring for or interested in them where practicable and appropriate (MCA s4(7); Winspear).

test.q: Which case established that failing to consult a mother before placing a DNACPR on her son, who lacked capacity, breached Article 8?
options: Montgomery
Tracey
Winspear
Gillick
test.why: Winspear v City Hospitals Sunderland (2015): failing to consult the mother when practicable was procedurally flawed and breached Article 8.

whyNot.0: Montgomery concerns disclosure of material risks.
whyNot.1: Tracey concerned consulting a patient who had capacity.

explain.body: IMCA (MCA s37) for serious medical treatment when there is no one but paid carers to consult. Welfare LPA covers life-sustaining treatment only if expressly stated. ADRT for life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed and say it applies even if life is at risk.

test.q: A man with a learning disability lacks capacity and has no family or friends. He needs a decision about major surgery. What must the NHS body do?
options: Ask his support workers to decide
Proceed in best interests without anyone else
Apply to the Court of Protection first
Instruct an IMCA before the decision
test.why: MCA s37: instruct an IMCA before serious medical treatment where there is no one, other than paid carers, appropriate to consult.

whyNot.0: Paid carers do not count as appropriate to consult.
whyNot.1: Best interests decisions need consultation; here that is an IMCA.
whyNot.2: Court is not the default route.

explain.body: DNACPR applies only to CPR. All other appropriate treatment and care continue, including escalation, unless separately decided.

test.q: A woman with a valid DNACPR develops a urinary infection. What does the DNACPR mean for her treatment?
options: No antibiotics can be given
Comfort care is all she can receive
Her family must agree to treatment
Usual treatment continues as needed
test.why: DNACPR relates only to CPR; appropriate treatment of other conditions continues.

whyNot.1: DNACPR is not a comfort-care-only order.
whyNot.2: It does not transfer treatment decisions to family.
